children.title: Organic Chemistry Reactions: Nucleophilic Substitution and Addition

concepts.title: The SN2 Mechanism
concepts.content: In the SN2 (concerted, bimolecular) mechanism the nucleophile attacks the electrophilic carbon at the same instant the leaving group departs, so bond making and bond breaking happen in one step. Attack comes from the backside, opposite the leaving group, passing through a pentavalent transition state and inverting the configuration at a chiral carbon. The rate is second order, first order in both nucleophile and substrate, and the reaction is fastest for unhindered methyl and primary alkyl halides bearing good leaving groups such as the heavier halides.

concepts.title: Acidity and Enolization
concepts.content: Protons on the carbon alpha to a carbonyl are unusually acidic because a strong base such as hydroxide or an alkoxide can remove one to give a resonance-stabilized carbanion, the enolate ion, whose negative charge is delocalized onto the electronegative carbonyl oxygen. The enolate is nucleophilic mainly at that alpha-carbon rather than at the oxygen. Because the alpha-carbon becomes trigonal and planar in the enolate, a stereocenter there can be racemized, and a proton flanked by two carbonyl groups is especially acidic.

concepts.title: Nucleophilic Addition Reactions to Aldehydes and Ketones
concepts.content: Because the carbonyl double bond of an aldehyde or ketone is strongly polarized, the carbonyl carbon is electrophilic and readily attacked by nucleophiles. In a nucleophilic addition the nucleophile bonds to that carbon while the pi bond breaks and the oxygen picks up the electrons to become an alkoxide, which is then protonated to an alcohol. The same electrophilicity makes these carbonyls easy to reduce, and many nucleophiles (hydride, organometallics, alcohols, amines, cyanide) add to them.

choices: attack by the amine nitrogen on the carbonyl carbon.
deprotonation of an alpha-hydrogen in cyclohexanone.

concepts.title: Esterification Reactions
concepts.content: In a Fischer esterification a carboxylic acid and an alcohol combine under acid catalysis to give an ester plus water. The transformation is a reversible equilibrium, so it is pushed toward the ester by using an excess of one reactant or by removing water. In the mechanism the acid first protonates the carbonyl to make its carbon more electrophilic, the alcohol adds to form a tetrahedral intermediate, and loss of water then delivers the ester; transesterification follows the same pattern with an alcohol replacing an alkoxy group.

problems.prompt: The acid-catalyzed reaction between methyl benzoate and propanol is a(n):
choices: reversible reaction, producing propyl benzoate and methanol.
reversible reaction, producing methyl propanoate and benzyl alcohol.
irreversible reaction, producing propyl benzoate and methanol.

concepts.title: Amino Acid Structure and Nomenclature
concepts.content: Every amino acid is built on a central alpha carbon bonded to an amino group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen, and a variable R-group (side chain) that distinguishes the twenty standard amino acids. Near physiological pH the amino group is protonated and the carboxyl is deprotonated, so the molecule exists as a dipolar zwitterion. Except for glycine, the alpha carbon is a stereocenter, and it is only the side chain that sets each amino acid's size, polarity, and charge.

concepts.title: The Peptide Bond
concepts.content: A peptide bond is the amide linkage formed by a condensation between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of the next, releasing water and joining residues into a chain that runs from a free N-terminus to a C-terminus. Delocalization of the nitrogen lone pair into the carbonyl gives the C-N bond partial double-bond character, so the unit is planar and rigid and usually adopts the trans configuration. Peptide bonds are kinetically stable but can be cleaved by hydrolysis, which proteolytic enzymes catalyze at specific residues.

problems.prompt: Partial hydrolysis of hexapeptide A gave four tripeptides; only one migrated toward the negative terminal during gel electrophoresis at pH 7. Which sequence is hexapeptide A?

concepts.title: Structure and Nomenclature of Monosaccharides
concepts.content: Monosaccharides are single sugar units with the general formula (CH2O)n, classified by chain length (triose, pentose, hexose) and by whether the carbonyl is an aldehyde (aldose) or a ketone (ketose). Each carries several hydroxyl groups and one or more stereocenters, so sugars occur as many stereoisomers, including enantiomers and epimers. In water a five- or six-carbon sugar cyclizes when one of its hydroxyls attacks the carbonyl, forming a hemiacetal ring and creating a new stereocenter at the anomeric carbon.

problems.prompt: Predict the product(s) of the reaction shown (an aldehyde treated with Cu2+ under basic aqueous conditions). (Choose the structure.)

concepts.title: Structure and Nomenclature of Disaccharides
concepts.content: A disaccharide is two monosaccharide units joined by a glycosidic bond, an acetal linkage formed between the anomeric carbon of one sugar and a hydroxyl of the other with loss of water. The linkage is specified by the carbons it connects and the anomeric configuration, for example a beta-1,4 bond, and different linkages give distinct disaccharides such as lactose, maltose, and sucrose. Acid- or enzyme-catalyzed hydrolysis cleaves the glycosidic bond and regenerates the two component monosaccharides.

concepts.title: Kinematics
concepts.content: Kinematics describes how objects move without addressing what causes the motion, using the quantities displacement, velocity, and acceleration. Displacement is the vector change in position, distinct from the scalar distance traveled; velocity is the rate of change of displacement, and acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, and each is a vector that can point in any direction. When acceleration is constant, these quantities are related by the standard kinematics equations linking displacement, initial and final velocity, acceleration, and time.

problems.prompt: A ball is thrown horizontally with initial velocity vx from a height Y. How long does it take to reach the ground (negligible air resistance, gravitational acceleration g)? (Choose the expression.)
Which of the following kinematic descriptions is physically impossible?
choices: An object in motion for a time interval has zero average velocity but positive nonzero average speed.
An object maintains constant speed for a time interval but has nonzero acceleration.
An object in motion for a time interval has zero displacement but nonzero total distance.
An object in motion for a time interval has an average velocity with a greater magnitude than its average speed.

problems.prompt: An object is projected from the ground at 30 degrees above the horizontal and returns to the ground 8 seconds later. What is its maximum height?
choices: There is not enough information to solve.

problems.prompt: Assuming one-dimensional motion, which velocity-time graph represents an object making a round trip? (Choose the graph.)

concepts.title: Mass, Force, and Newton's Laws
concepts.content: Mass measures an object's inertia, its resistance to changes in motion, whereas a force is a push or pull that can change an object's velocity. Newton's first law says an object keeps a constant velocity unless a net external force acts on it; the second law states that the net force equals mass times acceleration (F = ma), so acceleration grows with net force and shrinks with mass; the third law says every force is matched by an equal and opposite force exerted on the other object. Weight is simply the gravitational force on a mass, w = mg.

problems.prompt: Two lead balls of unequal mass are thrown vertically on the Moon, one directly up and one down at the same speed. Which statement(s) is/are true? I. Both reach the ground with the same speed. II. Both reach the ground at the same time. III. Both are attracted to the Moon with a force of equal magnitude.
Which best explains why one can drive faster without skidding around a banked curve than around a level curve?
choices: The greater vertical component of normal force on the banked curve increases the maximum frictional force, which increases the maximum centripetal force.
The additional horizontal component of normal force on the banked curve combines with friction to increase the maximum centripetal force.
The additional horizontal component of gravity on the banked curve combines with friction to increase the maximum centripetal force.
The reduction of the gravitational force on the banked curve means less centripetal force is required than on a level road.

choices: impossible to determine without knowing the densities

problems.prompt: Based on the tabulated coefficients of friction, which of the following can be validly concluded?
choices: Lubrication has a more significant effect on the coefficient of static friction than on kinetic friction.
If the static coefficient for one pair of materials exceeds that of another pair, the kinetic coefficient will always follow the same pattern.
The coefficient of kinetic friction is always less than or equal to the coefficient of static friction.
None of the above can validly be concluded from the given data.

concepts.title: Contact Forces: The Normal Force, Friction, and Tension
concepts.content: When two objects touch, they exert contact forces on each other. The normal force acts perpendicular to the surface and prevents objects from passing through it, while friction acts parallel to the surface and opposes sliding. Static friction, which can rise up to a maximum of the static coefficient times the normal force, keeps surfaces from starting to slide, whereas kinetic friction equals the kinetic coefficient times the normal force once sliding occurs, and the kinetic coefficient is usually smaller than the static one. Tension is the pulling force transmitted along a rope, string, or cable.

problems.prompt: A nurse inserts a catheter into a patient. To minimize discomfort and shearing damage, what should the nurse do?
choices: Squeeze harder and avoid lubricant to increase the coefficient of friction between the catheter and tissue.
Squeeze harder and use lubricant to decrease the coefficient of friction between the catheter and tissue.
Squeeze softer and avoid lubricant to increase the force of friction between the catheter and tissue.
Squeeze softer and use lubricant to decrease the force of friction between the catheter and tissue.

problems.prompt: When a copper pin slides against a copper surface, the force required to keep the pin sliding at constant speed is most likely:
choices: greater at high speeds than at low speeds.
greater at low speeds than at high speeds.

(Rubber's coefficient of friction decreases with greater normal force.)

concepts.title: Center of Mass, Torque, and Equilibrium
concepts.content: The center of mass is the mass-weighted average position of an object, the point that moves as though all of the object's mass and the net external force were concentrated there. Torque is the rotational effect of a force, equal to the force times its lever arm, the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the force's line of action, and it tends to cause angular acceleration. An object is in equilibrium when both the net force and the net torque on it are zero, so it has neither linear nor rotational acceleration.

problems.prompt: In the figure, the system is in static equilibrium. What is the force of static friction between block M and the inclined plane if M = 16 kg, m = 10 kg, theta = 30 degrees, and mu_s = 0.4?

The biceps tendon attaches about 3 cm from the elbow joint; a dumbbell is held about 30 cm from the elbow. With the elbow bent at 90 degrees and the forearm's weight neglected, what is the relation of the biceps force to the dumbbell's weight? (Choose the expression.)

concepts.title: Work
concepts.content: Work is done when a force acts on an object as it moves, and for a constant force it equals the component of the force along the displacement times the distance moved (W = Fd cos theta). Work is a scalar, measured in joules, and can be positive, negative, or zero: positive when the force has a component along the motion, negative when it opposes the motion, and zero when the force is perpendicular to the displacement. Work is the process by which energy is transferred to or from an object.

problems.prompt: Boxes of the same mass are lifted to a height of 3 m either up a frictionless ramp (Force F_A) or with a pulley (Force F_B). Which method requires more work?
choices: Equal work is required for both methods.
Greater work is required to lift m with the pulley.

choices: The mechanical advantage of the hill is half that of the double pulley system.

It is impossible to answer without knowing how far up the hill a person walked or how high a mass was lifted.

concepts.title: Kinetic Energy
concepts.content: Kinetic energy is the energy an object has because of its motion, given by KE = (1/2)mv^2, so it increases with mass and with the square of the speed and is never negative. The work-energy theorem states that the net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy (W_net = change in KE). Because of the speed-squared dependence, doubling an object's speed quadruples its kinetic energy.

problems.prompt: Which expression represents the kinetic energy of an object after it slides a distance d down a plane inclined at angle phi, with a constant frictional force F, starting from rest? (Choose the expression.)
A 1000 kg car traveling at 20 m/s brakes to a stop over a distance of 20 m. Assuming a constant kinetic frictional force, what is its magnitude?

concepts.title: Potential Energy
concepts.content: Potential energy is stored energy an object has by virtue of its position or configuration. Gravitational potential energy near Earth's surface is PE = mgh, so it changes with height, and only changes in potential energy are physically meaningful because the zero level is chosen arbitrarily. Gravity is a conservative force, meaning the work it does depends only on the change in height and not on the path taken, so gravitational potential energy converts freely to and from kinetic energy.

problems.prompt: Two friends slide down two frictionless slides to the same pool, one nearly vertical and one longer with a gentler slope. Which best describes their trips from start to finish?
choices: Both reach the pool in the same time and at the same final speed.
The vertical-slide friend reaches the pool in the same time but at a greater final speed.
The vertical-slide friend reaches the pool in less time but at the same final speed.

choices: It is impossible to tell without knowing the mass of the empty pail.

problems.prompt: Jack throws a non-uniform block of mass m from the peak of the hill. Neglecting air resistance, which statements is/are true? I. The center of mass follows a parabolic trajectory until it strikes the ground. II. Assuming it rotates, it rotates about its geometric center. III. The total displacement from throw to landing depends on the block's mass.

concepts.title: Total Mechanical Energy
concepts.content: An object's total mechanical energy is the sum of its kinetic and potential energy, E = KE + PE. When only conservative forces such as gravity do work, total mechanical energy is conserved, so any decrease in potential energy appears as an equal increase in kinetic energy and vice versa. When a nonconservative force such as friction acts, mechanical energy is not conserved, and the work done by that force equals the change in total mechanical energy.

problems.prompt: A basketball player jumps straight up for a slam dunk. Neglecting air resistance, which statements correctly describe the motion on the way up? I. Total mechanical energy is conserved. II. The player's weight increases as he rises. III. The work being done by gravity is negative.
An object is launched from the top of a 40 m high building with a speed of 10 m/s at 30 degrees above the horizontal. With what speed does it hit the ground?

Alexey jumps from a height of 20 m onto a seesaw and launches Boris 10 m into the air; both weigh 1000 N. Which could contribute to why Boris is not launched to 20 m? I. Alexey lands vertically but Boris launches off at a 45-degree angle. II. Alexey starts with 20 kJ of PE while Boris starts with 0 kJ. III. Not all kinetic energy is transferred from Alexey to Boris through the seesaw.
In which of the following real-world cases is total mechanical energy most nearly conserved?
choices: A sled sliding down an icy bobsled track
A pitched baseball being hit by a bat
A car with the driver slamming on its brakes to avoid a collision

concepts.title: Systems, Thermal Physics, and Thermodynamics
concepts.content: A thermodynamic system is the object or objects under study together with the ways they interact, while everything outside it is the environment; a system is open if it exchanges both matter and energy, closed if it exchanges only energy, and isolated if it exchanges neither. Thermal (internal) energy is the total random molecular motion within a system, temperature is the macroscopic measure of that energy per particle, and heat is thermal energy transferred between a system and its environment because of a temperature difference. Temperature is an intensive property that does not depend on the amount of material, whereas thermal energy is extensive.

problems.prompt: Jointed steel railroad track (coefficient of linear expansion 1.0e-5 per degC) was laid in 25 m sections at 4 degC with a 10 mm expansion joint. What must the track temperature be when the expansion joint closes?
About how much heat will a person release through evaporation on a relaxing day when they do not notice any perspiration? (L = 2.43e6 J/kg; roughly 0.6 kg of moisture is lost from the skin daily.)

A person sitting at room temperature (25 degC) with half their body covered has a basal metabolism generating 85 W of heat. About what percentage of that 85 W is lost through radiation? (k_rad about 5.6 W/(m^2 K), body area about 2 m^2, skin about 34 degC.)
For a perfectly insulated system, what are the values of the change in internal energy (delta-E_internal) and the heat Q if W = +100 J (the system does 100 J of work)?

concepts.title: The Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics
concepts.content: The zeroth law states that if two systems are each in thermal equilibrium with a third system, then they are in thermal equilibrium with one another. Thermal equilibrium means heat is free to pass between the bodies but no net heat flows, which happens precisely when they are at the same temperature, so the law establishes temperature as a consistent, measurable state variable. Bodies reach thermal equilibrium through heat transfer, which occurs by conduction (molecular collisions), convection (bulk motion of a fluid), and radiation (electromagnetic waves).

problems.prompt: On a hot, sunny, windless day you lie on a towel on the sandy beach and feel much warmer after a few minutes. What best explains this?
choices: The hot sand transferred heat into you by conduction and the Sun's rays transferred heat into you by radiation.
The hot sand transferred heat into you by conduction and the hot air transferred heat into you by convection.
The hot sand transferred heat into you by convection and the Sun's rays transferred heat into you by radiation.
All of your accumulated heat came from conduction by the surrounding air.

problems.prompt: Based on the thermoregulation passage, what best explains why people tend to cover most of their bodies with clothing in the winter?
choices: To increase the heat created by the body
To increase heat loss through conduction
To reduce heat loss through conduction
To reduce heat loss through radiation and convection

problems.prompt: Why are people who accidentally fall into cold water instructed to remain as still as possible while awaiting assistance?
choices: Remaining still reduces the heat generated in the body through metabolism.
Remaining still reduces the rate of heat loss via conduction.
Remaining still reduces the rate of heat loss via convection.
Remaining still reduces the rate of heat loss via radiation.

problems.prompt: During circulation, relatively warm blood moves from the heart to the extremities, where it cools slightly before returning to the heart. What best describes this process?
choices: This is a free convection process, as warm blood rises to the head while relatively cold blood sinks to the feet.

This is a free convection process, as the expansion of the warm blood in the heart pushes blood out to the extremities via the arteries, whereas cooler blood at the extremities condenses and sinks toward the heart via the veins.

This is a forced convection process where the pumping action of the heart forces blood heated by the body's metabolic processes out to the extremities, which in turn forces the cooler blood back toward the heart.
This is a forced convection process where the pumping action of the heart compresses and thereby heats the blood, and its motion to the extremities is a result of this pressurization.

concepts.title: The First Law of Thermodynamics
concepts.content: The first law is a statement of energy conservation: the internal energy of a system changes only through the heat added to it and the work it exchanges with the surroundings, written delta-E = Q - W in the physics sign convention (Q positive when heat flows in, W positive when the system does work on its surroundings). Energy may be transformed from one form to another, but the total energy of the universe is constant. For an ideal gas the internal energy depends only on temperature, and the work done by an expanding gas is W = P(delta-V), so in a constant-volume (isochoric) process no work is done and delta-E = Q.

problems.prompt: A mole of ideal gas undergoes an isochoric process. Which of the following quantities remains constant?
choices: the change in internal energy, delta-E

problems.prompt: An astronaut connects a full, well-insulated oxygen tank (at maximum pressure) to an identical, evacuated tank and opens the valve. What are the work W done by the oxygen in filling the second tank and the change in internal energy delta-E after it occupies both tanks?

A perfectly insulated, frictionless piston of gas starts at 2 kPa and 0.1 m^3 and runs a reversible cycle 1-2-3-4 back to its starting point (see the P-V diagram). What is the net work done by the gas over the cycle?
To raise the temperature of an ideal gas while adding the lowest possible amount of heat and doing no work on the gas, which process should you use?

concepts.title: The Second Law of Thermodynamics
concepts.content: Entropy is a measure of a system's disorder, and the second law states that the total entropy of an isolated system never decreases during any real process; a local decrease in entropy is possible only if the surroundings' entropy increases by at least as much. Because friction and other losses make real macroscopic processes irreversible, entropy tends to increase, which sets a direction for spontaneous change. As a result, heat flows spontaneously from a hotter body to a colder one but not the reverse without an input of work, and no cyclic engine can convert absorbed heat entirely into work.

problems.prompt: To cool your coffee, you drop an ice cube into a thermos (which prevents heat transfer in or out), seal it, and wait for the cube to melt. Which best describes the situation during the waiting period?
choices: The total energy of the system (coffee + ice) decreased and the entropy remained constant.
The total energy of the system and the entropy both remained constant.
The total energy of the system decreased and the entropy increased.
The total energy of the system remained constant and the entropy increased.

problems.prompt: According to the thermoregulation passage, if the ambient temperature rises above skin temperature, what best describes what happens to a person?
choices: Since heat cannot transfer from lower to higher temperature, body temperature rises, culminating in heat stroke.
The core temperature initially rises, so the body radiates more heat to the environment, cooling the core back within range.
Perspiration increases, as evaporation becomes the only heat-loss mechanism available to keep the core within range.
The body reduces the heat it generates through metabolism to keep the core within range.

problems.prompt: An ideal gas is held under pressure in an isolated container behind a thin membrane separating it from vacuum, like an inflated balloon in a large evacuated room. If the membrane is suddenly ruptured, what happens next?
choices: Nothing: the membrane ruptures, but the gas is unaffected.
The pressure and temperature both decrease rapidly.
The temperature decreases rapidly, but the pressure stays constant.
The pressure decreases rapidly, but the temperature remains constant, since no heat is exchanged and no work is done.

problems.prompt: A patient recovering from surgery is confined to a bed with minimal movement for the first couple of days; during that time, incisions heal and organ function returns to normal. What best explains this?
choices: Entropy of the person decreases but the entropy of the surroundings increases more.
Because the person does no work, she is an isolated system and thus her entropy increases.
The person absorbs more heat from the environment than she emits, and therefore is able to increase her internal energy.
There is no change to the entropy in the person because healing is a closed thermodynamic cycle.
